## 14 CFR § 91.151 — VFR fuel reserve for airplanes, beyond the first point of intended landing

### 1. Answer

| Condition of flight | Fuel required **after** reaching the first point of intended landing |
|---|---|
| Day, VFR, airplane | **30 minutes** at normal cruising speed |
| Night, VFR, airplane | **45 minutes** at normal cruising speed |

Both figures are minimum **times**, not distances or gallons, and both are computed at **normal cruising speed**, taking wind and forecast weather conditions into account.

### 2. Controlling text (quoted)

14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B — Visual Flight Rules, § 91.151 *Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions*:

> **§ 91.151 Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions.**
> (a) No person may begin a flight in an airplane under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed—
> (1) During the day, to fly after that for at least 30 minutes; or
> (2) At night, to fly after that for at least 45 minutes.

Text verified as identical in the current eCFR rendering of § 91.151 and in the 2025 printed CFR (Title 14, vol. 2) XML, retrieved 2026-11-15. Cite as **14 CFR § 91.151(a)(1)–(2)**.

### 3. What the rule actually requires (elements an inspector or reviewer checks)

1. **Airplane, VFR conditions.** The paragraph governs airplanes operating under VFR. (Rotorcraft are handled separately — see § 5.)
2. **Measured from the first point of intended landing.** The reserve is *in addition to* the fuel needed to arrive at that point; it is not the total fuel load.
3. **Expressed as time at normal cruising speed.** The regulation sets a duration, not a quantity. Convert to fuel using the airplane's normal cruise fuel flow; convert to still-air distance using normal cruise TAS.
4. **Wind and forecast weather must be considered.** This qualifies the whole requirement: the fuel plan must reflect the winds and forecast conditions expected, not a zero-wind best case.
5. **Applies when the flight is begun.** The prohibition is on beginning a flight without the required fuel; compliance is established at dispatch/takeoff, not adjusted in flight.

### 4. Applying it — worked conversion

Reserve fuel = reserve time × normal cruise fuel flow. Reserve still-air distance = reserve time × normal cruise TAS.

Example: airplane cruising 120 KTAS burning 10 gal/h.

| | Reserve time | Still-air distance | Fuel |
|---|---|---|---|
| Day | 0.50 h | 60 NM | 5.0 gal |
| Night | 0.75 h | 90 NM | 7.5 gal |

Total fuel at brake release = trip fuel to first point of intended landing (wind-adjusted) **+** the day or night reserve above. The reserve is a **regulatory minimum**; it is not an operating plan, and § 91.3 makes the pilot in command responsible for ensuring the actual fuel aboard is adequate for the flight.

**Day/night determination.** § 1.1 defines *night* as the period between the end of evening civil twilight and the beginning of morning civil twilight, and *day* as the period between the beginning of morning civil twilight and the end of evening civil twilight, as published in the U.S. Air Almanac. Use those times for the departure and destination, not colloquial sunrise/sunset. Where a flight will be airborne at night, plan the 45-minute reserve; that is the conservative and customary reading of a paragraph written in terms of the condition under which the flight is begun, and it is the reading any enforcement action would apply.

### 5. Adjacent and commonly confused rules (outside the question, flagged so they are not conflated)

- **§ 91.151(b) — rotorcraft:** 20 minutes at normal cruising speed after the first point of intended landing, with no day/night split. This is *not* the airplane answer.
- **§ 91.167 — IFR:** 45 minutes after the first point of intended landing (plus alternate fuel where § 91.169 requires an alternate). Same 45-minute figure as night VFR, different rule and different applicability; it does not answer a VFR question.
- **§ 135.209 — Part 135 VFR:** 30 minutes day / 45 minutes night, i.e., the same values as § 91.151. A Part 135 operator is not given relief by § 91.151; the two align on VFR reserves.
- **§ 91.205 — instruments/equipment:** requires a fuel gauge; it does not set a reserve quantity.

### 6. Scope and currency notes

- Answer assumes the current, generally applicable text of § 91.151 as published by the FAA; the 30-minute day / 45-minute night values are long-standing and are unchanged in the editions checked. For an official filing, cite the section and note the retrieval date.
- Answer is for **airplanes**; the request specified airplanes and § 91.151(a) is the airplane paragraph.
- Answer is informational — the regulatory minimum — and is not a compliance determination for any specific flight; the fuel actually required for a given flight may be higher once wind, forecast weather, alternates, and holding are accounted for.

disagreements.answer: 30 minutes during the day; 45 minutes at night

MEMORANDUM — RIGHT OF RESCISSION: EXERCISE DEADLINE AND OUTSIDE EXPIRATION UNDER 12 CFR § 1026.23(a)(3)(i)

I. QUESTIONS PRESENTED

1. Under 12 CFR § 1026.23(a)(3)(i), until when may a consumer exercise the right to rescind a covered credit transaction?
2. Under the same provision, when does that right expire if the required notice of the right to rescind or the material disclosures are never delivered?

II. SHORT ANSWERS

1. Three business days. The consumer may exercise the right until midnight of the third business day following the LAST to occur of: (a) consummation; (b) delivery of the notice required by § 1026.23(b); or (c) delivery of all material disclosures. "Business day" for rescission purposes means all calendar days except Sundays and the legal public holidays listed in 5 U.S.C. 6103(a) — so Saturdays count.

2. Three years. If the required notice or the material disclosures are never delivered, the right expires 3 years after consummation, or upon transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property, or upon sale of the property — whichever of those three occurs FIRST. The three-year mark is an absolute ceiling, not a floor, and the consumer does not have to sue to exercise the right within it.

III. CONTROLLING TEXT

12 CFR § 1026.23(a)(3)(i) provides:

"(i) The consumer may exercise the right to rescind until midnight of the third business day following consummation, delivery of the notice required by paragraph (b) of this section, or delivery of all material disclosures, whichever occurs last. If the required notice or material disclosures are not delivered, the right to rescind shall expire 3 years after consummation, upon transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property, or upon sale of the property, whichever occurs first. In the case of certain administrative proceedings, the rescission period shall be extended in accordance with section 125(f) of the Act."

Statutory backstop: 15 U.S.C. § 1635(f) (TILA § 125(f)) — "An obligor's right of rescission shall expire three years after the date of consummation of the transaction or upon the sale of the property, whichever occurs first, notwithstanding the fact that the information and forms required under this section or any other disclosures required under this part have not been delivered to the obligor."

IV. ANALYSIS OF ASK 1 — THE THREE-BUSINESS-DAY WINDOW

A. The three trigger events and the "last to occur" rule.

The clock does not start automatically at consummation. Section 1026.23(a)(3)(i) names three candidate events and keys the start to whichever occurs LAST:

  Event 1 — consummation;
  Event 2 — delivery of the notice required by § 1026.23(b);
  Event 3 — delivery of all material disclosures.

Practical consequence: if the notice and all material disclosures are delivered at or before consummation, the window runs from consummation and closes three business days later. If either is delivered after consummation, the window re-anchors to that later delivery date, and the consumer gets a fresh three business days from it. Where notice and disclosures are delivered on different dates, the clock starts on the later of the two.

B. "Material disclosures."

For rescission purposes, "material disclosures" means the annual percentage rate, the finance charge, the amount financed, the total of payments, and the payment schedule, as described in § 1026.18. Delivery of a disclosure statement that is materially inaccurate or incomplete is not treated by practitioners as satisfying the "delivery of all material disclosures" trigger, so the extended period continues to run. (Cite-check: the definitional sentence sits in § 1026.23(a)(3)(ii); confirm the subsection number against the current eCFR text before quoting it in a filing.)

C. "Midnight" and the day of the event.

The right is exercisable through the end of the third business day — midnight. The day on which the triggering event occurs is not counted; counting begins the next day. This is the standard Reg Z counting convention and it is the convention the industry applies to § 1026.23(a)(3)(i).

D. "Business day" for rescission — § 1026.2(a)(6).

Section 1026.2(a)(6) defines business day generally as a day on which the creditor's offices are open to the public for carrying on substantially all of its business functions, but expressly overrides that for rescission under §§ 1026.15 and 1026.23: for rescission, a business day is ALL calendar days except Sundays and the legal public holidays specified in 5 U.S.C. 6103(a) (New Year's Day, Martin Luther King, Jr. Day, Washington's Birthday, Memorial Day, Independence Day, Labor Day, Columbus Day, Veterans Day, Thanksgiving Day, Christmas Day).

Three consequences that drive real deadline errors:
  - Saturdays ARE business days for rescission counting (unlike the general Reg Z definition).
  - Sundays and federal holidays are excluded and do not count toward the three.
  - The creditor's own closing schedule, branch hours, or weather closures are irrelevant to the count.

E. Worked counting examples (all assume no later delivery of notice or disclosures).

  Ex. 1 — Consummation Monday March 3. Count Tue 4 (1), Wed 5 (2), Thu 6 (3). Right expires midnight Thu March 6.
  Ex. 2 — Consummation Friday. Count Sat (1), Sun excluded, Mon (2), Tue (3). Right expires midnight Tuesday. (Note the Saturday counts.)
  Ex. 3 — Consummation Wednesday. Count Thu (1), Fri (2), Sat (3). Right expires midnight Saturday.
  Ex. 4 — Consummation Thursday; notice delivered Friday; material disclosures delivered the following Tuesday. Last event = Tuesday. Count Wed (1), Thu (2), Fri (3). Right expires midnight Friday.
  Ex. 5 — Consummation Wed July 2, with July 4 (Friday) a federal holiday. Count Thu July 3 (1); Fri July 4 excluded; Sat July 5 (2); Sun July 6 excluded; Mon July 7 (3). Right expires midnight Monday July 7.

F. Scope predicate.

The three-business-day window presupposes a transaction actually subject to § 1026.23 — a consumer credit transaction in which a security interest is or will be retained or acquired in the consumer's principal dwelling, and not within the exemptions of § 1026.23(f) (e.g., a "residential mortgage transaction" as defined in § 1026.2(a)(24), or a refinancing by the same creditor to the extent of the existing unpaid principal balance plus costs). If the transaction is exempt, there is no federal rescission right and neither deadline applies. Ask 1 is answered on the assumption, stated in the request context, that the transaction is covered.

V. ANALYSIS OF ASK 2 — THE THREE-YEAR OUTSIDE EXPIRATION

A. Trigger condition.

The extended/outside period is triggered only "if the required notice or material disclosures are not delivered." Non-delivery — not late delivery — is the operative condition. Once triggered, the right does not simply run forever; it expires on the FIRST of three events:

  Event 1 — 3 years after consummation;
  Event 2 — transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property;
  Event 3 — sale of the property.

Because these are joined by "whichever occurs first," the three-year mark is a CEILING, not a guaranteed minimum. A sale or a transfer of all of the consumer's interest in year one terminates the right immediately.

B. Measuring the three years.

The three years are measured from the date of consummation. Consummation on June 15, 2022 produces an outside expiration at midnight June 15, 2025 (subject to the transfer/sale cutoffs above). The three-year period is not extended by the creditor's later curing of the disclosure defect, and it is not tolled by the consumer's ignorance of the violation.

C. The three years is absolute — Beach and Jesinoski.

  - Beach v. Ocwen Federal Bank, 523 U.S. 410 (1998): § 1635(f) is a statute of repose; after three years the right of rescission is completely extinguished and cannot be asserted as a defense or by recoupment.
  - Jesinoski v. Countrywide Home Loans, Inc., 574 U.S. 259 (2015): the consumer exercises the right by giving written notice of rescission within the three-year period; no lawsuit need be filed within the period. The notice, not the complaint, stops the clock.

So the correct formulation of the answer to Ask 2 is: the right expires at the earlier of (i) three years after consummation, (ii) transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property, or (iii) sale of the property — and written notice delivered on or before that moment is timely even if suit follows later.

D. Interaction with the three-business-day rule — the edge case.

If the notice and material disclosures are delivered late but still within three years, the consumer's window re-anchors to the delivery date under Ask 1 and runs three business days from it. If that late delivery occurs within the last three business days before the three-year mark, the two rules collide. The correct resolution is that the three-year mark controls as an absolute ceiling: the consumer cannot exercise the right after three years from consummation regardless of when the cure was delivered. Do not compute a rescission window that extends beyond the three-year date.

E. Administrative proceedings.

Section 1026.23(a)(3)(i) further provides that "[i]n the case of certain administrative proceedings, the rescission period shall be extended in accordance with section 125(f) of the Act." If the consumer is in a covered administrative proceeding, check § 1635(f) and the implementing provision before applying the ordinary three-year date.

F. Litigated boundary.

Whether a particular event is a "sale of the property" or a "transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property" for purposes of cutting off the right (for example, a foreclosure sale, a tax sale, or a payoff-and-refinance by a new lender) is a fact-bound question that the text does not resolve. It does not affect the two values stated here, both of which are taken directly from the regulation's own terms.

VI. HOW TO APPLY THIS — SEQUENCE

Step 1. Confirm coverage: consumer credit transaction, security interest in the consumer's principal dwelling, not exempt under § 1026.23(f).
Step 2. Fix the three candidate trigger dates: consummation date; date the § 1026.23(b) notice was delivered; date all material disclosures were delivered.
Step 3. If all three were delivered, take the latest date and count forward three rescission business days (skip Sundays and 5 U.S.C. 6103(a) holidays; count Saturdays). The right expires at midnight of the third such day.
Step 4. If the notice or material disclosures were never delivered, the window stays open, but only until the first of: three years after consummation, transfer of all of the consumer's interest, or sale of the property.
Step 5. If delivery occurred late, run Step 3 from the late delivery date but cap the result at the three-year date from Step 4.
Step 6. Confirm in writing that the consumer's own rescission notice was delivered on or before the computed deadline; under Jesinoski, written notice within the period is the exercise.

VII. CITATION NOTES AND LIMITS

  - This memorandum answers only § 1026.23(a)(3)(i) as asked. It does not address state-law rescission rights, which may run longer or shorter and are not preempted in this respect.
  - Two points should be cite-checked against the current eCFR and the Official Interpretations before use in a filing, because the researched source set did not include them: (a) the subsection number of the "material disclosures" definitional sentence (believed to be § 1026.23(a)(3)(ii)); and (b) whether any mailing/delivery presumption applies to the creditor's delivery of the notice and disclosures for purposes of starting the three-business-day clock. Neither point changes the two values stated in Section II.
  - Not legal advice; a compliance/legal analysis of the regulatory text for the general rule, not an opinion on any specific transaction.

CLASS 3 FLAMMABLE LIQUID — FLASH POINT THRESHOLD UNDER 49 CFR § 173.120(a)

1. ANSWER (both units and the comparison)

   Flash point threshold: 60 °C (140 °F).
   Comparison operator: "not more than" — i.e., AT OR BELOW (inclusive, ≤).

   A liquid is a Class 3 flammable liquid if its flash point is ≤ 60 °C (≤ 140 °F).

   Boundary reading, stated explicitly because inclusive/exclusive is where most mis-citations occur:
   - Flash point exactly 60 °C (exactly 140 °F)  -> IS Class 3.
   - Flash point below 60 °C (below 140 °F)      -> IS Class 3.
   - Flash point above 60 °C (above 140 °F)      -> is NOT Class 3 under the general rule in (a).
   "Not more than 60 °C" must not be restated as "below 60 °C"; the two differ at the boundary point.

2. GOVERNING TEXT (verbatim, 49 CFR § 173.120(a))

   "(a) Flammable liquid. For the purpose of this subchapter, a flammable liquid (Class 3) means a liquid having a flash point of not more than 60 °C (140 °F), or any material in a liquid phase with a flash point at or above 37.8 °C (100 °F) that is intentionally heated and offered for transportation or transported at or above its flash point in a bulk packaging, with the following exceptions:"

   Citation: 49 CFR Part 173, Subpart D, § 173.120(a).
   Verified against: eCFR current text (title-49/subtitle-B/chapter-I/subchapter-C/part-173/subpart-D/section-173.120) and the GovInfo CFR-2025-title49-vol2 XML/PDF of §173.120. Both print the same figure and the same operator; no conflicting threshold appears in the sources consulted.

3. UNIT CONSISTENCY CHECK

   60 °C x (9/5) + 32 = 140 °F exactly. The parenthetical in the regulation is an exact equivalent, not a rounded one, so there is no tolerance band to apply: the °C and °F statements of the threshold coincide. Quote the pair as printed — "60 °C (140 °F)" — rather than converting on the fly, so the citation stays verifiable against the text.

4. SECOND CLAUSE IN THE SAME SENTENCE (do not conflate with the threshold)

   Independently of the 60 °C test, §173.120(a) also captures "any material in a liquid phase with a flash point at or above 37.8 °C (100 °F) that is intentionally heated and offered for transportation or transported at or above its flash point in a bulk packaging." This is an alternative route into Class 3 for heated materials; it is not a second numeric threshold and does not modify 60 °C (140 °F). Keep it out of any answer to "what flash point defines Class 3" — the defining figure remains 60 °C (140 °F).

5. SCOPE NOTES AND VERIFICATION ITEMS

   - The definition in (a) is expressly "with the following exceptions"; §173.120(a)(1)–(3) carve out certain liquids (e.g., materials meeting the section's criteria for non-support of combustion or water-miscibility at stated flash points). Those exceptions are qualifications on the general rule, not alternate thresholds; cite them only if the question reaches them. They should be read in the current eCFR text before being quoted, since this answer does not reproduce them.
   - §173.120(b) defines the combustible liquid range above the flammable threshold. That upper figure is deliberately omitted here so that no number in this answer can be mistaken for the Class 3 threshold. If a downstream document needs it, pull it directly from (b) and label it as combustible, not flammable.
   - Flash point is the closed-cup value determined by the test methods referenced in Part 173 (see §173.121 for the assignment/test-method provisions). Confirm the specific method designations against the current text before putting a method number in a shipping paper or training document; open-cup results are not the regulatory basis.
   - Currency: this reflects the CFR text as published in the eCFR/GovInfo sources above. Before relying on it in a filing, confirm no amendment has issued since that text, per the standard check for Part 173.

6. ONE-LINE CITABLE FORM

   "Class 3 (flammable liquid): a liquid having a flash point of not more than 60 °C (140 °F) — 49 CFR § 173.120(a)."

WORKING TIME REGULATIONS 1998 (SI 1998/1833), REGULATION 4(1) — THE 48-HOUR AVERAGE LIMIT AND THE WRITTEN OPT-OUT

1. SHORT ANSWER
(1) Limit: a worker's working time, overtime included, must not exceed an average of 48 hours for each seven days, measured over the reference period applicable to that worker's case (reg 4(1)). This is an average, not a hard weekly ceiling: individual weeks may exceed 48 hours provided the average over the reference period does not.
(2) How a worker is taken outside it: by the employer first obtaining the worker's agreement in writing to perform such work — the individual 'opt-out' in regulation 5(1). Where a valid written agreement exists (and the employer meets the reg 5(4) record-keeping requirement), the reg 4(1) limit does not apply to that worker.

2. ASK 1 — THE LIMIT (reg 4(1), verbatim as fetched)
"4.—(1) [F1Unless his employer has first obtained the worker's agreement in writing to perform such work], a worker's working time, including overtime, in any reference period which is applicable in his case shall not exceed an average of 48 hours for each seven days."
Source: https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/1998/1833/regulation/4 (fetched 2026-11-15T09:39:09Z, sha256 b3d5adc6dca2).
Elements to state when applying it:
- Figure: 48 hours.
- Base: average for each seven days (i.e. a 7-day denominator, not per calendar week worked).
- Scope: 'working time, including overtime' — overtime is expressly inside the cap; unpaid overtime that counts as working time is not excluded.
- Measurement window: 'any reference period which is applicable in his case' — the limit is applied to an average across that period, not week by week.
- Persons: 'worker' (reg 2 definition), adult workers; young workers are subject to separate provisions and are outside this answer.

3. ASK 2 — THE MECHANISM (reg 5(1), verbatim as fetched)
"5.—(1) The limit specified in regulation 4(1) shall not apply in relation to a worker who has agreed with his employer in writing that it should not apply in his case, provided that the employer complies with the requirements of paragraph (4)."
Source: https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/1998/1833/part/II/made?view=plain (fetched 2026-11-15T09:39:10Z, sha256 19ee02c0047a).
Procedure, in the order the regulation requires:
Step 1 — Individual, not collective: the exclusion operates worker by worker. It is not a workforce or collective agreement varying the reference period; it is a personal agreement that the limit 'should not apply in his case'.
Step 2 — In writing: the agreement must be in writing. An oral agreement, or conduct implying consent, does not satisfy reg 5(1) (nor the F1 words in reg 4(1): 'agreement in writing to perform such work').
Step 3 — Obtained before the work is performed: reg 4(1) as amended reads 'Unless his employer has first obtained the worker's agreement in writing to perform such work' — the employer must obtain the agreement first, before the worker performs work beyond the limit.
Step 4 — Employer must satisfy reg 5(4): the disapplication is conditional ('provided that the employer complies with the requirements of paragraph (4)'). Per the researched summary, reg 5(4) obliges the employer to keep up-to-date records of workers who have agreed to opt out. If the employer does not comply, the reg 5(1) disapplication is not made out on the face of the text.
Step 5 — Effect: for that worker the reg 4(1) limit does not apply. The worker remains covered by the rest of the Regulations (night-work limits, rest breaks, annual leave, health assessments), which are not disapplied by reg 5(1).

4. PROVENANCE — WHAT IS VERIFIED AND WHAT IS NOT
(a) Verified verbatim from the fetched text: the words of reg 4(1) quoted at 2; the words of reg 5(1) quoted at 3; the existence of the reg 5(4) condition (referenced inside reg 5(1)).
(b) Reported by the research summary but NOT verified verbatim in the fetched passages — verify against the current text before publishing: that reg 4(2) fixes the reference period; that reg 5(4) is the up-to-date-records duty; that reg 4(2) itself imposes a 'reasonable steps' duty on employers for workers still within the limit.
(c) Not verified at all and deliberately not asserted as law in this answer: the length of the reference period (the 1998 Regulations as made used 17 weeks, extendable by collective/workforce agreement — confirm reg 4(2) and the extension provision); the worker's right to terminate the opt-out on notice and any cap on the notice period; the anti-detriment and unfair-dismissal protections for a worker who refuses to sign; the categories of worker who cannot rely on the opt-out or who are outside reg 4 altogether (civil aviation, sea, road transport and other excluded sectors under the later Parts of the Regulations); and the position of offshore workers.

5. CITATION AND AMENDMENT CAUTION
- Reg 4(1) carries an amendment marker ([F1]); the version quoted above is the amended form in which the written-agreement carve-out sits inside reg 4(1) as well as in reg 5(1). Cite the version in force at the date of the advice, not the 'as made' text, or the answer will read as though the limit were absolute.
- The Regulations have been amended repeatedly since 1998; re-verify regs 4 and 5 against legislation.gov.uk at the date of use.

6. SCOPE
This is a statement of the law as written for adult workers to whom reg 4 applies, not legal advice on any particular employment. Young workers, excluded sectors, and the record-keeping, detriment and dismissal consequences flagged in 4(b)–(c) are outside the two questions asked and are identified only so the reader knows what has not been covered.

question: P13
answer:
ANSWER (29 CFR § 825.200(a))

| Ask | Answer |
|---|---|
| 1. How much FMLA leave is an eligible employee entitled to (excluding care for a covered servicemember)? | 12 workweeks |
| 2. Over what period? | Any 12-month period |

The two figures are one entitlement, not two: 12 workweeks of leave per 12-month period. It is a ceiling for the period, not a grant that renews on each qualifying event and not a balance that carries over.

1. CONTROLLING TEXT

29 CFR § 825.200(a) provides:

"(a) Except in the case of leave to care for a covered servicemember with a serious injury or illness, an eligible employee's FMLA leave entitlement is limited to a total of 12 workweeks of leave during any 12-month period for any one, or more, of the following reasons:"

The paragraph then lists the qualifying reasons (birth and care of a child; placement of a child for adoption or foster care; the employee's own serious health condition; care of a spouse, son, daughter, or parent with a serious health condition; and a qualifying exigency arising out of covered active duty or call to covered active duty status).

Two operative words control the answer:

- "limited to a total of 12 workweeks" — the entitlement is a maximum, measured in workweeks, for all listed reasons combined. Taking leave for two or more qualifying reasons in the same period does not produce 12 weeks per reason.
- "during any 12-month period" — the measuring window is 12 months long. Section 825.200(a) fixes the length of the period but does not itself select which 12-month window applies; that is governed by § 825.200(b) (see Part 4).

2. WHAT THE 12 WORKWEEKS COVERS, AND WHAT IT DOES NOT

In scope of § 825.200(a) (all counted against the single 12-workweek total):
- birth of a child and care of the newborn;
- placement of a child for adoption or foster care;
- the employee's own serious health condition;
- care of a spouse, son, daughter, or parent with a serious health condition;
- a qualifying exigency arising out of a family member's covered active duty or call to covered active duty.

Excluded by the terms of the question and by the opening clause of (a):
- leave to care for a covered servicemember with a serious injury or illness (military caregiver leave). That is a separate entitlement under § 825.127, measured on its own terms, and it is not part of the 12-workweek figure above. It neither adds to nor alters the 12 workweeks stated for the reasons in scope.

Also outside the 12-workweek computation: FMLA's prohibitions on interference and retaliation (§ 825.220) and the employer's ability to provide more generous leave under a policy, CBA, or state law. FMLA leave is a floor; § 825.200(a) caps the statutory entitlement, not a more generous employer plan.

3. "ELIGIBLE EMPLOYEE" — WHY THE ANSWER IS STATED CONDITIONALLY ON STATUS

The 12-workweek entitlement in (a) belongs to an "eligible employee." Under § 825.110 that generally requires: (i) employment with the employer for at least 12 months (need not be consecutive); (ii) at least 1,250 hours of service in the 12 months immediately preceding the leave; and (iii) employment at a worksite where the employer employs 50 or more employees within 75 miles. The question stipulates eligibility, so these are noted only as the predicate; they do not change the 12 workweeks.

4. THE 12-MONTH PERIOD — HOW IT IS FIXED

Section 825.200(a) says "any 12-month period." Section 825.200(b) supplies the permitted ways to define that window. An employer may use any one of:
1. the calendar year;
2. any fixed 12-month "leave year" (fiscal year, a year required by state law, a year beginning on the employee's anniversary date);
3. a 12-month period measured forward from the date the employee's first FMLA leave begins; or
4. a "rolling" 12-month period measured backward from the date the employee uses any FMLA leave.

Rules that go with the choice (see § 825.200(b)–(c) and DOL Fact Sheet #28H):
- The chosen method must be applied consistently and uniformly to all employees.
- If the employer has not selected a method, the method that provides the most beneficial outcome to the employee applies.
- The method may be changed only with adequate notice to employees (DOL guidance: 60 days) and only if the change does not reduce an employee's existing entitlement.

Consequence for the answer to ask 2: the period is always 12 months long, but which 12 months can change how much leave is available on a given date, because leave already used inside the applicable window counts against the 12 weeks. Under method (4) — rolling backward — the balance at any moment is 12 workweeks minus all FMLA leave taken in the preceding 12 months. Example: an employee takes 4 weeks in March and 4 weeks in July; at the July request, 8 workweeks fall inside the look-back window, so 4 workweeks remain for the rest of that window. Under method (1) or (2), the balance resets at the start of the fixed year regardless of when the leave was taken.

5. HOW THE 12 WORKWEEKS IS COUNTED

- "Workweek" means the employee's normal workweek, not a flat 5-day or 40-hour unit for everyone. A full-time employee on a 40-hour week has 12 x 40 = 480 hours; an employee on a 20-hour week has 12 x 20 = 240 hours. These are arithmetic conversions of the same 12 workweeks, not additional leave.
- Intermittent or reduced-schedule leave is counted against the same 12 workweeks, in increments of the time actually taken (see § 825.205). Using leave intermittently does not increase the total.
- For employees with an irregular schedule, hours are computed under § 825.205; the 12-workweek ceiling is unchanged.
- Spouses who both work for the same employer share the 12 workweeks for certain reasons (birth, placement, and care of a healthy newborn or newly placed child) under § 825.202; the total for the couple is still 12 workweeks for those reasons, not 24.

6. PROCEDURE FOR APPLYING THIS TO A FILE

Step 1. Confirm eligible-employee status under § 825.110 (12 months, 1,250 hours, 50/75). If not eligible, the 12 workweeks does not apply.
Step 2. Identify the employer's selected 12-month method under § 825.200(b). If none is documented, apply the method most beneficial to the employee and note the absence.
Step 3. Establish the applicable 12-month window for the requested leave date.
Step 4. Total FMLA leave already used inside that window (all reasons in scope, including intermittent and reduced-schedule usage, converted to workweeks or hours on the employee's normal schedule).
Step 5. Remaining entitlement = 12 workweeks minus Step 4. Floor at zero; the figure cannot be negative and cannot exceed 12.
Step 6. Record separately, and do not net against the 12 weeks, any military caregiver leave taken under § 825.127.

7. COMMON ERRORS THIS ANSWER GUARDS AGAINST

- Treating the 12 weeks as available per qualifying event, yielding 24 or 36 weeks in one 12-month period. Wrong: (a) says "a total of 12 workweeks ... for any one, or more" of the reasons.
- Treating the 12 weeks as a balance that carries over or accrues. Wrong: the entitlement is per 12-month period.
- Assuming § 825.200(a) mandates a particular 12-month window (e.g., calendar year). Wrong: (a) fixes the 12-month length; (b) supplies the four permissible methods.
- Folding military caregiver leave into the 12 weeks, or adding it to the 12 weeks to produce a combined figure in this analysis. Wrong for this question: it is expressly carved out of (a) and governed by § 825.127.

ANSWER — 14 CFR § 91.151(a), fuel reserves for an airplane under VFR

An airplane may not begin a flight under VFR conditions unless, considering wind and forecast weather conditions, it carries enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and then, at normal cruising speed, to continue for:

  • Day:   at least 30 minutes beyond the first point of intended landing.
  • Night: at least 45 minutes beyond the first point of intended landing.

| Condition | Reserve beyond the first point of intended landing | Expressed as |
|---|---|---|
| Day (VFR, airplane) | 30 | minutes at normal cruising speed |
| Night (VFR, airplane) | 45 | minutes at normal cruising speed |

GOVERNING TEXT (verbatim, § 91.151(a))

"(a) No person may begin a flight in an airplane under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed—
(1) During the day, to fly after that for at least 30 minutes; or
(2) At night, to fly after that for at least 45 minutes."

Authority: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, § 91.151, "Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions." Text as maintained on eCFR (https://ecfr.gov/current/title-14/section-91.151), fetched 2026-11-15T09:41:05Z, sha256 a8a7e00944fb; corroborated by the 2025/2026 GovInfo CFR volumes for 14 CFR 91.151.

HOW THE FIGURE IS APPLIED

1. Compute trip fuel to the first point of intended landing, applying wind and forecast weather conditions as the rule requires (i.e., headwind/tailwind and forecast temperature affect the fuel actually needed to get there).
2. Add the reserve on top of that: 30 minutes (day) or 45 minutes (night), at normal cruising speed. The reserve is fuel remaining after arrival at the first point of intended landing — it is not part of the fuel to that point.
3. Total minimum fuel to begin the flight = trip fuel to first point of intended landing + reserve.

Converting the reserve time to fuel: the regulation fixes a time, not a quantity. Convert using the planned normal cruising speed and the corresponding cruise fuel burn. Example at 120 KTAS: 30 min ≈ 60 NM, 45 min ≈ 90 NM; at a cruise burn of 10 gal/h, that is 5 gal (day) and 7.5 gal (night). Scale linearly with the aircraft's own cruise speed and burn.

"Normal cruising speed": the rule does not prescribe a single number; it means the speed at which the aircraft is expected to be operated in cruise on that flight (normally the planned cruise TAS used for flight planning). The reserve must be computed at that same speed, not at a slower holding speed and not at maximum speed.

"Night": for the 45-minute reserve, night has the meaning in 14 CFR § 1.1 — the period between the end of evening civil twilight and the beginning of morning civil twilight, as published in the Air Almanac and converted to local time. A flight that will be partly day and partly night should be planned to the night figure (45 minutes) to remain compliant.

SCOPE — WHAT THIS ANSWER DOES NOT COVER (so no competing number is implied)

• Rotorcraft: § 91.151(b) imposes a separate VFR reserve for rotorcraft. It is not an airplane rule and is outside this answer.
• IFR: § 91.167 governs IFR fuel (a different reserve and an alternate-airport requirement). Not applicable to a VFR flight.
• Part 121 / Part 135: §§ 121.639 and 135.209 impose their own VFR fuel rules on those certificate holders; this answer is the Part 91 rule.
• No VFR alternate fuel: Part 91 imposes no alternate-airport fuel requirement for VFR flight, so the only add-on beyond trip fuel is the 30/45-minute reserve above.

CURRENCY NOTE

The 30/45-minute figures reflect the current, in-force text of § 91.151 as of the fetch cited above; the section carries no delayed compliance date or alternative text. If the section is later amended, re-verify against the then-current eCFR text before relying on these numbers.

MEMORANDUM — RIGHT OF RESCISSION: EXERCISE DEADLINE AND EXPIRATION UNDER 12 CFR § 1026.23(a)(3)(i)

1. QUESTIONS PRESENTED
(1) Until when may a consumer exercise the right to rescind a covered credit transaction under 12 CFR § 1026.23(a)(3)(i)?
(2) When does that right expire if the required notice of the right to rescind or the material disclosures are never delivered?

2. SHORT ANSWERS
(1) Until midnight of the third business day following the last to occur of: (a) consummation of the transaction; (b) delivery of the notice of the right to rescind required by § 1026.23(b); or (c) delivery of all material disclosures. Answer value: 3 business days, ending at midnight.
(2) The right expires 3 years after consummation — unless, before that date, all of the consumer's interest in the property is transferred or the property is sold, whichever occurs first. Answer value: 3 years after consummation.

3. CONTROLLING TEXT (12 CFR § 1026.23(a)(3)(i))
"(i) The consumer may exercise the right to rescind until midnight of the third business day following consummation, delivery of the notice required by paragraph (b) of this section, or delivery of all material disclosures, whichever occurs last. If the required notice or material disclosures are not delivered, the right to rescind shall expire 3 years after consummation, upon transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property, or upon sale of the property, whichever occurs first."
Statutory anchor: 15 U.S.C. § 1635(f) (right of rescission expires three years after consummation or upon sale of the property, whichever occurs first, notwithstanding non-delivery of the required information and forms).
Official Interpretation to § 1026.23(a)(3)(i): "When the creditor has failed to take the action necessary to start the three-business day rescission period running, the right to rescind automatically lapses on the occurrence of the earliest of the following three events: A. The expiration of three years after consummation of the transaction." (followed by B. transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property; C. sale of the property).

4. ANALYSIS — ASK 1: THE EXERCISE DEADLINE
4.1 Structure of the rule. Subdivision (a)(3)(i) contains three independent triggering events, and the rescission clock starts on the LAST of them:
  (a) consummation;
  (b) delivery of the notice required by § 1026.23(b) (the notice of the right to rescind, two copies per § 1026.23(b)(1)); and
  (c) delivery of all material disclosures.
In the ordinary, compliant transaction all three occur at or before consummation, so the clock runs from consummation. If the creditor delivers the notice or any material disclosure after consummation, the clock does not start until that later delivery — the consumer is not penalized for the creditor's delay, and the period is not shortened by the earlier events.
4.2 The endpoint is "midnight of the third business day." The consumer must exercise before midnight at the end of the third business day counted from the triggering event. Exercise is by written notice to the creditor (15 U.S.C. § 1635(a); Jesinoski v. Countrywide Home Loans, Inc., 574 U.S. 259 (2015) — a written notice of rescission mailed within the period is effective; the consumer need not file suit within the period).
4.3 "Business day" for rescission purposes. Under § 1026.2(a)(6), for purposes of rescission under §§ 1026.15 and 1026.23, "business day" means all calendar days except Sundays and the legal public holidays specified in 5 U.S.C. § 6103(a) (e.g., New Year's Day, Martin Luther King, Jr. Day, Washington's Birthday, Memorial Day, Independence Day, Labor Day, Columbus Day, Veterans Day, Thanksgiving Day, Christmas Day). Saturdays therefore count; Sundays and those federal holidays do not.
4.4 Worked examples.
  Example A (compliant delivery at consummation). Consummation Monday, June 2, 2025; notice and all material disclosures delivered that day. Business day 1 = Tuesday, June 3; day 2 = Wednesday, June 4; day 3 = Thursday, June 5. The right may be exercised until midnight on Thursday, June 5, 2025.
  Example B (late delivery of the notice). Consummation Monday, June 2, 2025; material disclosures delivered at consummation, but the § 1026.23(b) notice is delivered Friday, June 6, 2025. The clock runs from June 6: day 1 = Saturday, June 7 (Saturday counts); Sunday, June 8 is excluded; day 2 = Monday, June 9; day 3 = Tuesday, June 10. The right may be exercised until midnight on Tuesday, June 10, 2025 — subject to the three-year ceiling in Part 5.
4.5 Limits on the rule. The three-business-day period is not extended by agreement, and the consumer may waive the right only in accordance with § 1026.23(a)(2) (a dated, signed written statement in a personal financial emergency, describing the emergency and specifying the waiver). A defective or incomplete notice or a missing material disclosure does not start the clock — it leaves the consumer in the never-delivered posture addressed in Part 5.

5. ANALYSIS — ASK 2: EXPIRATION WHERE NOTICE OR MATERIAL DISCLOSURES ARE NEVER DELIVERED
5.1 The three-year ceiling. If the creditor never delivers the § 1026.23(b) notice or never delivers all material disclosures, the right to rescind expires 3 years after consummation. This period is measured from the date of consummation — not from discovery, demand, tender, or any later delivery — and is expressed in years, not business days; it is not computed by excluding weekends or holidays.
5.2 The two earlier cutoffs. The three-year period is not the only limit. The right also expires, if earlier:
  (a) upon transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property (by any means, including a refinance payoff/deed transfer, divorce transfer, or conveyance to a trust); or
  (b) upon sale of the property.
The regulation and the Official Interpretation both state the rule as "whichever occurs first," so the operative date is the EARLIEST of the three-year anniversary, the transfer of all interest, and the sale.
5.3 The lapse is automatic. The Official Interpretation states that when the creditor has failed to start the three-business-day period running, the right "automatically lapses" on the earliest of the three events; no notice from the creditor, no demand, and no affirmative act is required to terminate it.
5.4 Effect of a late delivery that occurs before the three-year mark. If the creditor delivers the notice and material disclosures after consummation but before the right has lapsed, the consumer receives a fresh three-business-day rescission window running from that delivery (Part 4), but that window cannot extend the right past the three-year/transfer/sale ceiling. A delivery made after the right has already lapsed does not revive it.
5.5 Illustration. Consummation June 2, 2025; no notice and no material disclosures ever delivered; the consumer does not transfer all interest and the property is not sold. The right to rescind expires three years after consummation — June 2, 2028 — and a written notice of rescission delivered before that date is timely (Jesinoski). If the consumer instead conveys the property in full on March 1, 2027, the right expires on that earlier date.

6. "MATERIAL DISCLOSURES"
The term is defined for this purpose in § 1026.23(a)(3)(ii), which enumerates the core TILA disclosures (annual percentage rate, finance charge, amount financed, total of payments, payment schedule) together with the disclosures and limitations incorporated by cross-reference to § 1026.32(c) and (d) and § 1026.35(c)(2). Because the operative consequence of a missing material disclosure is to leave the consumer in the three-year posture of Part 5, the enumeration should be checked against the current text of § 1026.23(a)(3)(ii) at the time of any live matter; the core five items above are the ones that matter in the overwhelming majority of files.

7. SCOPE AND ASSUMPTIONS
  - The transaction is assumed to be one to which the rescission right actually attaches under § 1026.23(a)(1): consumer credit in which a security interest is or will be retained or acquired in the consumer's principal dwelling. The right does not apply to a residential mortgage transaction (purchase-money first lien) as defined in § 1026.2(a)(24), to business-purpose credit, or to the other exempt transactions in § 1026.23(a)(1)/(e). If the transaction is exempt, neither answer applies.
  - The answers state the rule as currently in force; the regulation text quoted above is unchanged in the versions retrieved (2020-12-28, 2023-05-15, and current eCFR).
  - The answers address the general rule; they do not address the § 1026.23(a)(2) emergency waiver, the effects of rescission under § 1026.23(d), or a creditor's civil liability for failing to honor a timely rescission.
  - Verify before reliance in a live matter: (i) the exact enumeration in § 1026.23(a)(3)(ii); (ii) the current text of the § 1026.2(a)(6) rescission business-day definition and the 5 U.S.C. § 6103(a) holiday list for the relevant year; (iii) the pin cite for the quoted Official Interpretation comment; and (iv) any state-law rescission right, which is unaffected by these federal ceilings.

8. SOURCES
  - 12 CFR § 1026.23(a)(3)(i) (current eCFR, https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-12/chapter-X/part-1026/subpart-B/section-1026.23).
  - Regulation Z § 1026.23 (CFPB, https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/2020-12-28/23/ and .../2023-05-15/23/).
  - Official Interpretations to § 1026.23 (https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/interp-23/).
  - Federal Reserve Regulation Z § 1026.23 (https://www.federalreserve.gov/frrs/regulations/section-102623-right-of-rescission.htm).
  - 15 U.S.C. § 1635(a), (f); Jesinoski v. Countrywide Home Loans, Inc., 574 U.S. 259 (2015).

Scope. This answer is for an adult worker in Great Britain under the Working Time Regulations 1998 (SI 1998/1833), as amended. Northern Ireland has its own parallel Working Time Regulations (Northern Ireland) 1998, which contain the same 48-hour average. Young workers and sector-specific regimes are outside this answer.

1. The limit. Regulation 4(1) provides that, unless the employer has first obtained the worker's agreement in writing to perform such work, the worker's working time, including overtime, in any reference period applicable to the worker must not exceed an average of 48 hours for each seven days. The statutory figure is therefore 48 hours per seven days, averaged over the applicable reference period. It is an average, not a hard cap on every individual week: a particular week can exceed 48 hours provided the average over the reference period remains at or below 48. The default reference period is 17 weeks (reg 4(3)); it may be extended by a collective agreement or workforce agreement to a maximum of 52 weeks (reg 4(4)).

2. The mechanism for taking a worker outside the limit. The regulation 4 route outside the limit is the individual written opt-out: the employer must first obtain the worker's agreement in writing to perform the work that would otherwise take the worker outside the 48-hour average. 'First' is substantive: the agreement must be obtained before the worker performs the relevant work; a retrospective agreement does not satisfy reg 4(1). The agreement must be genuine and voluntary, not imposed in a way that negates consent. The worker may terminate the agreement by notice under reg 5; in practice the statutory default is at least 7 days' notice, with a longer period (up to three months) only if the agreement so provides. A collective or workforce agreement can extend the reference period to 52 weeks, but it cannot substitute for the individual written agreement needed to disapply the 48-hour limit for a worker.

3. Employer duties. Under reg 4(2), the employer must take all reasonable steps, in keeping with the need to protect the health and safety of workers, to ensure the limit is complied with for workers to whom it applies, and must keep up-to-date records of all workers who carry out work to which the limit does not apply because the employer has obtained the written agreement. The opt-out does not remove other Working Time protections: daily rest, weekly rest, rest breaks, night-work limits, annual leave and health assessments continue to apply.

4. Practical procedure. (a) Calculate the worker's average working time over the applicable reference period, including overtime. (b) If the average is at or below 48, no opt-out is needed; if the employer needs the worker to work in a way that would exceed the average, obtain a written agreement before that work is performed. (c) The agreement should identify the work or arrangement, be signed and dated by the worker, and be retained. (d) Record the worker in the opt-out register and monitor hours and health and safety. (e) Allow the worker to withdraw on the statutory or contractual notice, and adjust scheduling accordingly.

Bottom line: the limit is an average of 48 hours per seven days, including overtime; a worker is taken outside that limit only if the employer first obtains the worker's written agreement to perform the work (the individual opt-out).

# FMLA Leave Entitlement Under 29 C.F.R. § 825.200(a) (Excluding Military Caregiver Leave)

## 1. Short answer

**Amount:** An eligible employee is entitled to a total of **12 workweeks** of FMLA leave. This is an aggregate cap covering any one or more of the qualifying reasons in § 825.200(a) — it is *not* 12 workweeks per qualifying reason.

**Period:** Those 12 workweeks are measured over **a 12-month period**, and the specific 12-month period is whichever of the four methods the *employer* has adopted under § 825.200(b): (1) the calendar year; (2) any fixed 12-month leave year; (3) the 12-month period measured forward from the date the employee's first FMLA leave begins; or (4) a rolling 12-month period measured backward from the date FMLA leave is used.

**Scope of the exclusion:** As requested, this answer excludes leave to care for a covered servicemember with a serious injury or illness. That separate entitlement (26 workweeks) is carved out by the opening clause of § 825.200(a) and is not part of the figures above.

## 2. Controlling text

**29 C.F.R. § 825.200(a)** (verbatim, as fetched):

> "(a) Except in the case of leave to care for a covered servicemember with a serious injury or illness, an eligible employee's FMLA leave entitlement is limited to a total of 12 workweeks of leave during any 12-month period for any one, or more, of the following reasons:"

**29 C.F.R. § 825.200(b)** (verbatim, as fetched):

> "(b) An employer is permitted to choose any one of the following methods for determining the 12-month period in which the 12 weeks of leave entitlement described in paragraph (a) of this section occurs:
> (1) The calendar year;
> (2) Any fixed 12-month leave year, such as a fiscal year, a year required by State law, or a year starting on an employee's anniversary date;
> (3) The 12-month period measured forward from the date any employee's first FMLA leave under paragraph (a) begins; or,
> (4) A 'rolling' 12-month period measured backward from the date an employee uses any FMLA leave as described in paragraph (a)."

Sources: https://ecfr.gov/current/title-29/section-825.200 ; https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2025-title29-vol3/xml/CFR-2025-title29-vol3-sec825-200.xml (both fetched 2026-11-15T09:45:47Z).

## 3. Analysis

### 3.1 The amount is 12 workweeks, and it is a single aggregate cap

Section 825.200(a) states a "total of 12 workweeks" for "any one, or more" of the enumerated reasons. Two consequences follow that are frequently misstated in practice:

- An employee who has, for example, both a serious health condition and a family member with a serious health condition does **not** get 12 weeks per reason. The cap is 12 workweeks combined.
- The entitlement is to *leave*, not to paid leave. Substitution of accrued paid leave (§ 825.207) runs concurrently with and counts against the 12 workweeks; it does not extend them.

### 3.2 "Workweek" means the employee's own normal workweek

The unit is the workweek, so the entitlement follows the employee's schedule rather than a fixed hour count. It is not prorated for part-time status — a part-time employee still has 12 workweeks, but each workweek contains fewer hours. Express regulatory conversion of the entitlement into hours/days is a mechanical step the employer performs for tracking purposes; the following is arithmetic, not a regulatory figure:

| Employee's normal workweek | 12 workweeks equals |
|---|---|
| 40 hours (5 x 8) | 480 hours / 60 workdays |
| 37.5 hours (5 x 7.5) | 450 hours / 60 workdays |
| 20 hours (part-time) | 240 hours / 60 workdays |
| Any schedule | 12 x (normal weekly hours) |

Each of these is exactly 12 workweeks; none exceeds or varies the regulatory cap. Where an employee's schedule varies week to week, the hours-equivalent is derived from the employee's normal/average hours, and the total may not exceed 12 workweeks of the employee's schedule.

### 3.3 The period is a 12-month period, defined by the employer's election

Section 825.200(b) does not impose one universal 12-month window; it authorizes four. The practical significance of the choice:

- **Calendar year** and **fixed leave year** are *fixed-window* methods. They permit "stacking" at a year boundary — leave taken at the end of one fixed window and the start of the next can yield more than 12 consecutive workweeks of leave.
- **Forward-measured from first leave** creates an individual anniversary cycle per employee, keyed to the first use of leave.
- **Rolling backward** looks back 12 months from each date leave is used; it is the method that prevents stacking, because a new block of leave only becomes available as old leave ages out of the look-back window.

The choice is the employer's, but it must be applied consistently and communicated to employees so that they can determine how much leave remains. **Verification note:** § 825.200 contains further provisions on consistent application, changing the method, and the consequence of an employer's failure to select any method (the option most beneficial to the employee). Those provisions are cited here from the regulation's structure but were **not** captured verbatim in the sources consulted for this answer, so no quotation of them is offered; confirm the exact paragraph text before relying on that specific point.

### 3.4 What the exclusion does and does not remove

The opening clause of § 825.200(a) removes only "leave to care for a covered servicemember with a serious injury or illness" — the military caregiver entitlement (26 workweeks in a single 12-month period, with its own per-servicemember limit). Everything else in § 825.200(a) remains inside the 12-workweek cap: birth and bonding, placement for adoption or foster care, the employee's own serious health condition, and care for a covered family member with a serious health condition. If the requester intended to exclude *all* military family leave (including qualifying exigency leave), that would change the framing but not the 12-workweek figure, because qualifying exigency leave is already counted within the 12 workweeks.

### 3.5 Things that do not change the 12 workweeks

- **Intermittent leave or a reduced work schedule** (§ 825.202): the leave may be taken in blocks or by reducing hours, but the total is still capped at 12 workweeks.
- **Substitution of paid leave** (§ 825.207): concurrent, counts against the 12 weeks.
- **Employer policy or collective bargaining agreement** providing more leave: that is contractual/statutory leave in addition to FMLA, not an enlargement of the FMLA entitlement.
- **State or local leave laws** that provide greater leave: FMLA is a floor; the state entitlement runs alongside, and the FMLA entitlement itself remains 12 workweeks.

### 3.6 Distinct from the amount: eligibility

Eligibility is a separate predicate, not part of the entitlement figure. An employee must have 12 months of service, 1,250 hours of service in the preceding 12 months, and work at a worksite with 50 or more employees within 75 miles (§ 825.110). The 12-workweek figure answers *how much* an **eligible** employee gets; it does not establish that any particular employee is eligible.

## 4. Limitations and open items (flagged, not assumed away)

1. **The employer's chosen method is not identified in the request.** The answer to "over what period" is "a 12-month period as the employer has elected under § 825.200(b)." Any employee-specific statement of how much leave remains on a given date requires that election plus the employee's leave-use history. That is a missing fact, not a gap in the legal answer.
2. **Special computation rules** apply to airline flight crew members (hours-of-service based computation) and to instructional employees (scheduling of leave). Those rules affect how the 12 workweeks is translated into hours or when leave may be scheduled; they do not alter the 12-workweek total. The specific section cites were not verified in the sources consulted and are therefore referenced by subject matter only.
3. **Currency:** the text quoted is the current eCFR/2025 CFR compilation. No pending amendment to § 825.200 is reflected in the sources consulted.
4. **Public-sector employers** are covered employers under the FMLA; the 12-workweek entitlement is unchanged, though separate federal leave systems (e.g., Title 5 / OPM-administered family leave) may provide parallel entitlements.

## 5. Authorities

- 29 C.F.R. § 825.200(a) — 12 workweeks per 12-month period; servicemember-care exception.
- 29 C.F.R. § 825.200(b)(1)-(4) — the four permissible 12-month period methods.
- 29 C.F.R. Part 825, Subpart B — amount and manner of leave (intermittent/reduced schedule, substitution, scheduling).
- 29 C.F.R. § 825.110 — eligibility prerequisites (separate from amount).

| Day | 30 minutes at normal cruising speed | § 91.151(a)(1) |
| Night | 45 minutes at normal cruising speed | § 91.151(a)(2) |

Both figures are expressed as time, exactly as the rule states them; they are not gallons, pounds, or nautical miles. Conversion to a quantity of fuel is a separate calculation using the aircraft's normal cruising fuel consumption (see Step 4).

1. GOVERNING TEXT (verbatim, § 91.151(a))
"(a) No person may begin a flight in an airplane under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed—
(1) During the day, to fly after that for at least 30 minutes; or
(2) At night, to fly after that for at least 45 minutes."

2. HOW THE FIGURES ARE APPLIED (procedure)
Step 1 — Identify the first point of intended landing. This is the first place the flight is intended to land, not necessarily the final destination; on a multi-leg VFR flight it is the first landing point of that leg/flight as planned. The reserve is measured after arrival at that point.
Step 2 — Compute the fuel needed to reach that point considering wind and forecast weather conditions. The rule makes wind and forecast weather part of the calculation, so the en-route fuel is not still-air fuel.
Step 3 — Add the reserve: 30 minutes if the flight is conducted during the day, 45 minutes if conducted at night, in each case at normal cruising speed (the speed actually used for cruise planning, not maximum-range or best-endurance speed).
Step 4 — Convert the reserve time to a quantity if a gauge/ramp figure is needed: reserve quantity = normal cruising fuel consumption (gal/hr or lb/hr) × reserve time in hours. Example: at a planned normal cruise of 120 KTAS, 30 min = 60 NM and 45 min = 90 NM; at 10 gal/hr normal cruise, 30 min = 5.0 gal and 45 min = 7.5 gal. (Illustrative arithmetic only; substitute the actual aircraft figures.)
Step 5 — The total from Steps 2–3 must be aboard when the flight begins. § 91.151 is written as a prohibition on beginning a flight, so the fuel must be present at takeoff, not merely planned to be acquired en route.

3. SCOPE AND EDGE NOTES
- Applicability: airplanes operating under VFR under Part 91. The 30/45-minute figures above answer the question as asked (airplane).
- Night: the 45-minute figure applies to a flight conducted at night. For reference, 'night' is defined in § 1.1 as the time between the end of evening civil twilight and the beginning of morning civil twilight as published in the Air Almanac, converted to local time. A flight that begins by day and continues into night should be planned to the night figure.
- Rotorcraft are governed by § 91.151(b), not § 91.151(a); that paragraph sets lower figures (summarized, not quoted: 20 minutes by day and 30 minutes at night). Those are context only and are NOT the answer to this request.
- IFR flights are governed by § 91.167, not § 91.151 (45 minutes beyond the destination or, when an alternate is required, beyond the alternate airport, at normal cruising speed). Not applicable here, given for cross-reference only.
- § 91.151 is a regulatory minimum. It does not displace § 91.3 (pilot in command's responsibility for the safety of the flight) or any operational need for additional fuel (e.g., anticipated delays, approaches, weather avoidance). Planning to exactly 30 or 45 minutes is planning to the floor, not to a prudent margin.
- No day/night boundary is defined inside § 91.151 itself; the day/night distinction is the regulation's own applicability trigger, with 'night' taking the § 1.1 definition above.

4. CITATION AND VERIFICATION
Authority: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, § 91.151, 'Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions.' Text quoted above verified against the current eCFR text of § 91.151 (eCFR, Title 14, section 91.151, fetched 2026-11-15T09:46:50Z, sha256 a8a7e00944fb) and consistent with the GovInfo CFR XML/PDF compilations of 14 CFR 91.151. No conflicting authoritative source was found.

BOTTOM LINE: Day VFR — 30 minutes beyond the first point of intended landing; Night VFR — 45 minutes beyond the first point of intended landing; both at normal cruising speed, both considering wind and forecast weather conditions, and both measured as fuel that must be aboard when the flight begins.

Scope and assumptions. This is a federal Regulation Z analysis under the current 12 CFR part 1026 text. 'Covered credit transaction' is not a defined term in Regulation Z; I read it as a transaction subject to the rescission right in § 1026.23—i.e., a consumer credit transaction in which a security interest is or will be retained or acquired in the consumer's principal dwelling and the consumer's ownership interest is or will be subject to that security interest (§ 1026.23(a)(1)), and not an exempt transaction under § 1026.23(f). No state-law overlay or transaction-specific facts are addressed.

Citation correction. The 'midnight of the third business day' rule is textually in § 1026.23(a)(2), not § 1026.23(a)(3)(i). Section 1026.23(a)(3)(i) supplies the expiration rule when the required notice or material disclosures are not delivered. The substance of the two asks is answered by reading (a)(2) and (a)(3)(i) together.

Ask 1—general and extended exercise deadline. Under § 1026.23(a)(2): 'The consumer may exercise the right to rescind until midnight of the third business day following consummation, delivery of the notice required by paragraph (b) of this section, or delivery of all material disclosures, whichever occurs last.' Therefore, the consumer may exercise the right until midnight of the third business day following the last of: (1) consummation; (2) delivery of the § 1026.23(b) notice; or (3) delivery of all material disclosures. If the notice and material disclosures are delivered at different times, the later delivery is the trigger; both the notice and all material disclosures must be delivered for the normal three-business-day period to run from delivery. For rescission, 'business day' means all calendar days except Sundays and the federal legal public holidays listed in 5 U.S.C. 6103(a) (§ 1026.2(a)(6)). The trigger is delivery, not merely mailing; use the delivery date under § 1026.23(b) and the official interpretations.

Ask 2—never delivered. Under § 1026.23(a)(3)(i): 'If the required notice or material disclosures are not delivered, the right to rescind shall expire 3 years after consummation, upon transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property, or upon sale of the property, whichever occurs first.' Therefore, if the required notice or material disclosures are never delivered, the right expires at the earliest of: (1) three years after consummation; (2) transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property; or (3) sale of the property. The three years run from consummation, not from discovery of the failure. If either the notice or the material disclosures are never delivered, the normal three-business-day period in (a)(2) never starts from that missing delivery, and the (a)(3)(i) outer limit controls.

Practical bottom line. Timely delivery: midnight of the third business day after consummation, or after the later delivery if notice/material disclosures are delivered after consummation. Late delivery: midnight of the third business day after the last required delivery. No delivery: earliest of 3 years after consummation, transfer of all the consumer's interest in the property, or sale of the property. The three-year period is an outer limit for non-delivery, not a free-standing three-year right when notice and material disclosures are timely delivered.

answer:
ANSWER (49 CFR § 173.120(a), Class 3 flammable liquid)

Threshold flash point: not more than 60 °C (140 °F).
Comparison: the definition is written as a ceiling — a liquid qualifies as a Class 3 flammable liquid if its flash point is AT OR BELOW 60 °C (140 °F) ('not more than'). A flash point above 60 °C (140 °F) does not meet the base definition in § 173.120(a).

1. CONTROLLING TEXT (verbatim, § 173.120(a), first sentence)

"(a) Flammable liquid. For the purpose of this subchapter, a flammable liquid (Class 3) means a liquid having a flash point of not more than 60 °C (140 °F), or any material in a liquid phase with a flash point at or above 37.8 °C (100 °F) that is intentionally heated and offered for transportation or transported at or above its flash point in a bulk packaging, with the following exceptions:"

Source: 49 CFR § 173.120, Title 49, Subtitle B, Chapter I, Subchapter C, Part 173, Subpart D — https://ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-B/chapter-I/subchapter-C/part-173/subpart-D/section-173.120 (eCFR 'current' text as fetched 2026-11-15T09:49:34Z; identical text appears in the GovInfo CFR-2025-title49-vol2 XML for sec. 173-120).

2. THE FIGURE IN BOTH UNITS, WITH THE CONVERSION SHOWN

- Metric (regulation's primary figure): 60 °C
- Customary (regulation's parenthetical): 140 °F
- Conversion check: °F = (°C × 9/5) + 32 = (60 × 9/5) + 32 = 108 + 32 = 140 °F. Exact, no rounding discrepancy.

Use the paired figures exactly as the regulation prints them — 60 °C (140 °F) — rather than re-rounding one from the other.

3. THE COMPARISON, STATED PRECISELY

- Operator: "not more than" = ≤.
- Qualifying: flash point ≤ 60 °C (≤ 140 °F) → Class 3 flammable liquid (subject to the exceptions in (a) and to (b) below).
- Boundary case: a liquid with a flash point of exactly 60 °C (140 °F) IS a Class 3 flammable liquid. The boundary is inclusive.
- Non-qualifying under (a): flash point > 60 °C (> 140 °F). Do not invert this — writing the rule as 'at or above 60 °C' inverts the definition and is the single most common error on this provision.

4. SECOND PRONG OF THE SAME DEFINITION (does not change the threshold)

Section 173.120(a) is a two-pronged 'or'. A material in a liquid phase with a flash point AT OR ABOVE 37.8 °C (100 °F) is still a Class 3 material if it is intentionally heated and offered for transportation, or transported, at or above its flash point in a bulk packaging. Conversion check: (37.8 × 1.8) + 32 = 100.04 ≈ 100 °F — this is the regulation's own rounded pairing, not an independent conversion.

Practical consequence for classification: 37.8 °C (100 °F) is NOT a second, lower Class 3 threshold. It is the floor of the heated-bulk-packaging prong. For a non-heated, non-bulk shipment the only figure that governs is 60 °C (140 °F). For a heated bulk shipment, test the material against the 37.8 °C (100 °F) prong and against whether it is offered/transported at or above its own flash point.

5. SCOPE — WHAT THIS ANSWER DOES AND DOES NOT COVER

- Covered: the base Class 3 flammable liquid definition, § 173.120(a), first prong.
- Not covered by this figure: § 173.120(b), the combustible-liquid provision, which is a separate provision addressing liquids above the flammable cut-off. Do not use (b) to answer the Class 3 question.
- Not covered: the enumerated carve-outs. Section 173.120(a) closes with 'with the following exceptions:'; those exceptions are part of the definition and can remove a ≤ 60 °C (≤ 140 °F) liquid from Class 3 (for example, liquids meeting another hazard class definition, and certain mixtures/solutions). Read § 173.120(a)(1) et seq. in the current text before applying the 60 °C screen to a specific material. This summary does not restate the exception text verbatim because only the lead-in sentence was captured in the verified passage.
- Test-method dependence: the quoted text of (a) states the figure without naming a flash-point test method in that sentence. Flash point values are method-dependent (open-cup vs. closed-cup; different apparatus give different numbers), and Part 173 references specific ASTM/ISO methods in the exceptions and related sections. Before classifying a material, confirm which method the governing text requires and report the flash point with its method. Do not compare an open-cup result to a closed-cup threshold without conversion/justification.
- Definitional dependence: § 173.120 uses 'flash point' as a defined term carried elsewhere in the subchapter; the threshold is only as good as the flash-point determination behind it.
- Currency: the figures above are from the eCFR 'current' text as of the fetch date noted. Confirm against the edition of 49 CFR your shipping papers/ERP are built on; the HMR are amended by harmonization rulemakings.

6. HOW AN ENGINEER VERIFIES THIS IN TWO MINUTES

1) Open 49 CFR § 173.120 on eCFR (or the GovInfo CFR volume for your year). 2) Read paragraph (a), first sentence; confirm 'not more than 60 °C (140 °F)' and the 'or ... 37.8 °C (100 °F) ... intentionally heated ... bulk packaging' clause. 3) Confirm the paragraph ends 'with the following exceptions:' and read (a)(1)–(a)(n) as printed. 4) Confirm paragraph (b) is the combustible-liquid provision and is not the source of your Class 3 answer. 5) Record the flash point of your material with the test method used, and apply: FP ≤ 60 °C (140 °F) → Class 3 under (a) first prong; otherwise check the heated-bulk prong; otherwise check (b).

7. ONE-LINE CITATION FORM

49 CFR § 173.120(a): Class 3 flammable liquid — flash point not more than 60 °C (140 °F); also a liquid-phase material with flash point ≥ 37.8 °C (100 °F) intentionally heated and transported at or above its flash point in a bulk packaging.
